planting.note: Plant grafted trees in late winter to early spring; Qing is a Chinese chestnut selection that bears precociously (often within 2-4 years) and needs a second, genetically distinct chestnut nearby for cross-pollination and full nut set. Space wide to accommodate a broad, spreading mature canopy and good air circulation in humid Gulf South summers.

directions: Plant two or more genetically distinct chestnut trees for reliable cross-pollination in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun. Qing is a widely planted Chinese chestnut cultivar selected for strong resistance to chestnut blight, dependable annual production, and a manageable, relatively compact tree form compared with seedling Chinese chestnuts; nuts are medium-large, glossy mahogany-brown, and sweet, dropping free of the burr for easy harvest in September-October. It is a mainstay of southern nut-orchard and food-forest plantings because it tolerates heat and humidity far better than American or European chestnut, sets a heavy crop at a young age, and shows good resistance to the ambrosia beetle and gall wasp pressure that troubles many other chestnut selections in the Gulf South.
sources: University of Missouri Center for Agroforestry — Chinese Chestnut Cultivar Trials
Auburn University College of Agriculture — Chestnut Growers Information

planting.note: Plant dormant, container-grown bushes in winter to early spring in highly acidic soil; Austin needs roughly 500-550 chill hours and ripens early-to-mid season. Plant with another rabbiteye cultivar such as Climax or Premier for cross-pollination and a heavier set.

directions: Plant in acidic soil (pH 4.5-5.2) amended with pine bark or peat and mulch heavily to keep roots cool and moist. Austin is a University of Georgia-released rabbiteye blueberry that ripens just after Climax in the early part of the season, producing medium-to-large, firm, light-blue berries with good flavor on a vigorous, upright bush. It extends the early harvest window when planted alongside Climax and Premier, and its dependable, heavy cropping habit combined with good disease tolerance has made it a standard early-season choice for Gulf South home orchards and u-pick plantings. Fertilize lightly with an acid-forming fertilizer in early spring and again after harvest, and prune out old, unproductive canes each winter to keep the bush renewing vigorous new fruiting wood.
sources: University of Georgia Cooperative Extension — Rabbiteye Blueberry Varieties
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Commercial Blueberry Production
Ison's Nursery and Vineyard variety notes

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root grafted trees in spring; Rossiyanka is a cross between the American persimmon (Diospyros virginiana) and the Oriental persimmon (Diospyros kaki) bred in Russia for extreme cold hardiness, tolerating winter lows to roughly -25 to -30°F once dormant while retaining the larger, less astringent fruit of its Asian parent.

directions: Plant in full sun in any well-drained soil; established trees are drought-tolerant and need little supplemental fertilization beyond a light annual feeding. Rossiyanka is a Russian-bred hybrid between the native American persimmon and the Asian kaki persimmon, developed to combine the extreme winter hardiness of the American parent with fruit size and eating quality closer to Asian types. The medium-large orange fruits are strongly astringent until fully soft-ripe, at which point they turn sweet and jammy with a rich, honeyed flavor; frost or a period of cold storage speeds the softening. Self-fruitful and reliably productive once established, it is a good choice for growers who want Asian-persimmon-quality fruit in a climate too cold, or on a rootstock too marginal, for standard kaki cultivars, and it also performs well in the milder Gulf South.
sources: One Green World Nursery — Hybrid Persimmon Cultivar Notes

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees or rooted hardwood cuttings in spring; in zone 9 plant February-April. Russian 26 is one of a group of cold-hardy pomegranate selections imported from the former Soviet Union, tolerating temperatures into the low teens °F once established. Self-fertile; no separate pollinator required.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil; pomegranates tolerate poor, alkaline, and clay soils far better than most fruit trees. Russian 26 is one of several numbered cold-hardy pomegranate cultivars brought into North American cultivation from Russia and Central Asia, prized for combining good winter hardiness with heavy, precocious production of medium-sized fruit. The rind is typically pink to red and the arils are juicy, sweet-tart, and well flavored, ripening in early-to-mid fall. Established plants are very drought-tolerant and long-lived, and the compact, multi-stemmed shrub form makes it easy to manage as a large shrub or small espaliered tree. In the Gulf South, Russian 26 fruits reliably and its cold tolerance provides insurance against occasional hard freezes that can damage less hardy pomegranate selections.
sources: California Rare Fruit Growers Association — Pomegranate Cultivar Comparison
Just Fruits and Exotics Nursery variety notes

common_name: Louisiana Ribbon Cane (Heirloom Striped Syrup Cane)

planting.note: Plant stalk sections (billets) with 2-3 nodes horizontally in a shallow furrow after last frost; in zone 9 plant February-April. Ribbon Cane is a traditional Gulf South heirloom variety grown chiefly for syrup rather than table sugar, prized for its distinctive green-and-purple striped stalks.

directions: Plant billets of two or three nodes in loose, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, keeping soil consistently moist through the growing season. Louisiana Ribbon Cane is a historic heirloom sugarcane variety, distinguished from modern commercial hybrids by its slender, green-and-purple striped stalks, that has been maintained by Deep South farm families and seed savers for generations specifically for making cane syrup rather than refined sugar. It is traditionally harvested in November and December after the first light frosts sweeten the stalks, then stripped, crushed, and the juice slow-cooked down into dark, richly flavored cane syrup, a staple of Louisiana and Georgia country cooking. The tall, clumping perennial grass also makes a striking, fast-growing screen or accent planting; in zone 9 it typically dies back to the rhizome after a hard freeze and regrows vigorously each spring.
sources: Louisiana State University AgCenter — Sugarcane Production and Heirloom Varieties
Southern Foodways Alliance — Cane Syrup Traditions
